Improvements and extensions in spDBL

Source: IMPROVEMENTS.md

This document lists what spDBL adds to the method of Banerjee, Chen, Frankenburg and Zhou (2025), Dynamic Bayesian Learning for Spatiotemporal Mechanistic Models, Journal of Machine Learning Research 26(146):1–43, and to the research code written for that paper (https://github.com/xiangchen-stat/Bayesian_Modeling_Mechanistic_Systems). It accompanies the submission of spDBL 1.2.0 to the JMLR Machine Learning Open Source Software track. The paper does not present spDBL, and the package has not been published elsewhere. Changes by version are in NEWS.md.

Starting point

  • The paper sets out the method:
    • a matrix-variate dynamic linear model emulator with exact forward filtering and backward sampling (FFBS), under inverse-Wishart and σ²R covariance models;
    • Gaussian-process interpolation over simulator inputs;
    • episode-wise processing of spatial blocks;
    • analytic log predictive densities;
    • Bayesian calibration with a dynamic spatial discrepancy, fitted by Metropolis-within-Gibbs.
  • The research code is a set of R and C++ scripts for the paper’s experiments, without a package structure or tests. Its calibration runs the simulator for every proposed parameter value. In dev/calibrate_EP_sigma2R.R, each Metropolis proposal calls update_muSigma_eta_one(), which solves the PDE with gen_pde(). The paper reports 59 minutes for one calibration of a 6 × 6 SIR model (30,000 draws).
  • spDBL 1.0.2, the first CRAN release (August 2026), packaged the emulator: emulator_learn(), emulator_predict(), the filters and samplers, out-of-core forward filtering, and the paper’s SIR simulator. It had no calibration interface.

Extensions of the method

  1. Calibration without simulator runs. calibration_prepare() fits a Gaussian process over the inputs that predicts the autoregressive design rows at untried parameter values, so the sampler never calls the simulator and its cost no longer depends on the simulator’s.
    • Since 1.2.0 the GP uses a Matérn 5/2 kernel with separate hyperparameters for each time step.
    • Its predictive variance enters the field covariance (design_uncertainty = TRUE, the default).
    • calibration_validate() checks it on held-out runs.
  2. Marginalised calibration with NUTS. calibration_fit() conditions on each emulator posterior draw and then:
    • integrates the emulated field out in closed form and the dynamic discrepancy by a Kalman filter;
    • samples only (η, τ²) with Stan’s NUTS;
    • recovers the fields and the discrepancy afterwards by exact Gaussian backward sampling (calibration_predict());
    • pools the conditional posteriors over emulator draws with equal weights (a modular, or “cut”, posterior: the field data do not update the emulator), reporting R̂, effective sample sizes and divergences for each.
    Two Stan programs, one with the discrepancy marginalised and one with it explicit, have R reference implementations of the same log densities.
  3. More general discrepancy: a positive-definite discrepancy covariance scale U with a non-unit diagonal (1.1.1).
  4. Emulator coefficient sampling either jointly along backward paths or from smoothed marginals (sampling = "joint" or "marginal"), recorded in saved objects (1.1.1).
  5. Exact prediction with fixed coefficient trajectories, cached factors and the conditional covariance (FFBS_predict_exact(), 1.1.0).
  6. Causal default autoregressive designs (1.2.0). A lag that does not exist yet is an intercept column, so early-time designs no longer use the response itself, random noise or future values.

Software

  • Interface. Seven workflow functions run the analysis:
    • prepare_data(), emulator_learn(), emulator_predict();
    • calibration_prepare(), calibration_validate(), calibration_fit(), calibration_predict().
    They return classed, serialisable objects (spDBL_emulator, spDBL_calibration_input, spDBL_calibration) with print() methods, and summary(), predict() or plot() methods where they apply. The filters, smoothers, samplers and predictors remain exported as building blocks for new emulators.
  • Large grids.
    • Emulators no longer build the dense S × S field kernel unless it is supplied, which removes an O(S³) step and O(S²) memory from every fit.
    • Out-of-core backward smoothing (BS_bigdata_R()) and prediction (FFBS_predict_bigdata_R(), posterior means) join forward filtering (FF_bigdata_R()), streaming CSV blocks. They match the in-memory versions; the workflow functions do not use them yet.
  • Reproducibility.
    • Functions that take a seed restore the caller’s random-number state.
    • Compiled Stan models are cached on disk, keyed by the program and the R, rstan and platform versions.
    • calibration_fit() can save each conditional fit as it completes.
    • Bundled datasets record their provenance.
    • An installed script reproduces the calibration example with recorded settings.
  • Model comparison. Analytical and draw-based WAIC for multivariate regression with inverse-Wishart covariance (1.1.2).
  • Fixes found by the new tests (1.2.0), among them:
    • the discount factor delta was accepted but ignored;
    • grid partitions overlapped or left rows uncovered in edge cases;
    • the paper-era calibration helpers could give a negative predictive variance near a training input.

Quality assurance and documentation

  • Tests.
    • Coverage is 99.1% of R and C++ lines (covr, with the Stan tests, in CI on the 1.2.0 release), up from 31% in 1.1.1.
    • Numerical components are checked against independent calculations: the filter against exact Gaussian conditioning, the Stan log densities against R code, and the samplers by their moments.
    • The Stan back end is also tested without compiling Stan.
  • Continuous integration. GitHub Actions run:
    • R CMD check on Ubuntu (R devel, release and the previous release), macOS and Windows;
    • test coverage with the Stan tests;
    • a license-header check;
    • the pkgdown build.
  • Documentation.
    • Every exported function has a runnable example.
    • Vignettes cover emulation, calibration, the calibration model in detail, and model comparison.
    • The website (https://xiangchen-stat.github.io/spDBL/) adds a grouped function reference and an architecture article for contributors.
    • A contributing guide, code of conduct, and issue and pull-request templates are in .github/.
  • Licensing. MIT; every hand-written source file carries an SPDX license header.

Benchmarks

Scripts, Slurm job files and raw results are in benchmarks/; benchmarks/README.md maps each result folder to the manuscript. The manuscript uses results/e1/paper, results/e2/fixed, results/e3/mode, results/e3_diagnostic and results/listing1.

  • Emulator scaling (E1). Training is closed form. With 10⁴ sites, fitting the inverse-Wishart emulator with 10 posterior draws takes 1.4 minutes and 13 GiB with episode window 1, and 15.5 minutes and 62 GiB with window 5; with emulator_learn(keep_draws = FALSE) peak memory falls to 9 and 33 GiB with identical results.
  • Emulator accuracy (E2). On a fixed 10 × 10 domain at three resolutions (10², 20², 50²), with 10 designs of 40 training and 50 held-out runs per grid, predictions at untried inputs made without simulator runs were compared with RobustGaSP (ppgasp) and a principal-component GP.
    • spDBL’s 95% intervals covered 94.5–95.8% of held-out values on every grid; the competitors’ covered 82–88%, less in 119 of the 120 design-paired comparisons.
    • The principal-component GP’s RMSE was lower by 0.014–0.026, within design-to-design variation; ppgasp’s was higher on every grid, significantly at 50².
    • The ablations in the same run show that the coverage comes from the per-time-step Matérn design GP: used alone it covers 94.6–94.9%, while ppgasp fitted per time step covers 85.5–87.6%. The dynamic model lowers the design GP’s RMSE by 1–1.5%.
    • Prediction takes 1 to 16 s for 50 runs (43 s to 15 minutes before the batched prediction of 1.2.0), against under a second for the competitors, and 5.3 GiB (2.4 GiB with regenerated draws) against 0.6-0.7 GiB at 50².
  • Calibration (E3). In 30 replicate calibrations against RobustCalibration (S-GaSP and GaSP discrepancies), every method’s chains started at its own optimum:
    • posterior means matched in accuracy (relative RMSE 0.100 against 0.107 and 0.118);
    • spDBL’s chains mixed better (median smallest bulk ESS 949 against 106 and 40; rank-normalised Rhat above 1.01 in 13 replicates against 30 and 30);
    • every method’s 95% intervals under-covered, spDBL’s most (54% against 60% and 67%). Ablations on 10 replicates trace this to the emulator’s systematic error, not the inference: with field data drawn from the emulator’s own model, spDBL’s intervals covered 93%, while joint coefficient paths and 60 emulator draws changed nothing. More training runs remove it: new designs of 40, 80 and 160 runs covered 77%, 83% and 93%, and the bundled 40 runs plus 40 placed near a first-stage posterior covered 100%;
    • no simulator runs were needed, whereas the research code solves the PDE at every proposal.
